p: Whitby Abbey has a starring role in English history, not just in Dracula. In 664, the Synod of Whitby met here and settled how the date of Easter would be worked out, a decision that shaped the church in England for centuries. The abbey is also linked with Caedmon, a cowherd who became the earliest named English poet, and a carved stone cross honouring him stands near the top of the 199 steps.

If the steps aren't for you, there's an English Heritage car park up on the headland itself, so you can drive straight to the abbey and skip the climb. It's worth knowing if you've got young children, a buggy or anyone with mobility worries in your group.

Back down in town, the Captain Cook Memorial Museum on Grape Lane is a fascinating stop. It's in the house where the young James Cook lodged as an apprentice, and it tells the story of his early life and his famous voyages. Over on the West Cliff, the whalebone arch frames the abbey across the harbour, giving you one of the town's best photographs.

Twice a year, Whitby Goth Weekend brings dramatic costumes and a buzzing atmosphere to the town, which can be a great spectacle but means busier streets and accommodation. Book early if you're planning a trip around then.
Robin Hood's Bay, a pretty fishing village, is just down the coast for a day trip, and steam trains on the North York Moors line connect to Whitby on selected days.
